title: The hands
hookLine: the cosmic mudra: left hand on right, thumbs lightly touching, an oval at the navel

cards: Hands are hardly ever off duty. Since waking they've probably held a phone, a cup, a door handle, a spoon; typed, scrolled, pointed, waved. Even resting, they fidget.
Sit down to meditate and they get restless: on the knees, then the thighs, then folded, then back on the knees. Zen gives them a job, a very small one, done resting in the lap.

teach.h: ONE HAND RESTING IN THE OTHER.
teach.b: In zazen the hands rest in the lap in what's often called the cosmic mudra. A mudra is a gesture held with the hands, sometimes called a seal.
The back of one hand rests in the palm of the other, fingers overlapping, the left on the right in the usual Soto Zen instruction. Dogen's guide to sitting gives it that way.

The tips of the two thumbs come up and just meet over the fingers, lightly. Some teachers say: as if holding a sheet of paper between them. Hands and thumbs make an oval that rests against the belly, near the navel.
The thumbs are a small gauge. If they press together into a peak, there's probably tension somewhere: effort, trying too hard.
If they sag apart into a valley, the mind may be getting dull or drowsy. So some teachers say: don't stare at the mind, check the thumbs. They show the strain before it's noticed anywhere else.
With the hands joined and resting, the arms can drop from the shoulders, and the fidgeting has nowhere to go.
The hands aren't asleep. They hold a shape that takes almost no effort and just a little attention.
Some statues of the Buddha seated in meditation show a resting gesture like this one, a way of saying with the body: nothing to grab right now, nothing to push away.

how: In Zen sitting, practitioners usually hold the hands in the cosmic mudra for the whole period, and teachers check beginners' hands along with their posture.

games.q: you're sitting, and you notice your thumbs have pushed hard into each other. what do the teachers suggest?
o: soften, and let them just touch
drop the mudra and let the hands hang
games.why: pressing thumbs often mean effort and tension. soften them back to just touching, and the rest of the body tends to follow.

practice: Sit upright and relaxed, lay one hand in the other, left resting on right, and bring the thumb tips up until they just touch, the oval resting near your belly.
Keep a little attention in the thumbs: if they press, soften; if they drift apart, gently bring them back. That's the whole job.

wordCard.voice: The hands. In zazen, the cosmic mudra: one hand resting in the other, thumbs lightly touching, an oval near the navel. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: thumbs just touching. A small shape, and a quiet gauge. See you tomorrow.
